findings.title: join() skips terminate() for remaining flusher processes when the deadline expires
findings.body: In SpanFlusher.join(), the loop over self.processes does `break` when `remaining_time <= 0`, which exits the for-loop before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for all processes that come after the one being waited on. With the old single-process code, terminate was always reached; now a timeout while waiting on the first process leaves every other flusher process unterminated. If any of those processes is hung (e.g. blocked in a Redis call) it keeps running after join() returns, continuing to flush and produce segments for shards that may have been reassigned to another consumer during the rebalance, risking duplicate segment production. The `break` should be a `continue` (skip the wait but still terminate), or terminate should be called for all remaining processes.

findings.title: Restarted flusher processes are killed but never joined, leaking zombies and IPC resources
findings.body: In _ensure_processes_alive(), an unhealthy process is killed via process.kill() and then immediately replaced by _create_process_for_shards(), which overwrites self.processes[process_index] with the new Process. The old Process object is never join()ed or otherwise reaped, and nothing else references it, so each restart leaves a zombie child and leaks its sentinel pipe/file descriptors on Linux. For a long-running consumer that recovers flusher processes periodically (the restart logic exists precisely for that), these accumulate over the process lifetime. The old process should be joined (with a small timeout) after kill before spawning the replacement.

findings.title: Redis memory usage is summed across per-shard-group buffers, potentially double-counting clusters
findings.body: submit() now computes Redis backpressure by extending memory_infos from every buffer in self.buffers and summing used/available across all entries. Previously a single SpansBuffer covering all assigned shards produced the memory info. If a Redis cluster is reachable from more than one shard-group buffer (shards mapping to the same cluster can be split across processes by the round-robin assignment in __init__), that cluster's ServiceMemory is counted once per buffer that touches it. This weights the used/available ratio by how many buffers reference each cluster rather than by actual memory, so the `spans.buffer.max-memory-percentage` threshold can trigger too early or too late. The per-cluster results should be deduplicated (e.g. keyed by cluster) before summing.

findings.title: Metric tag typo: wait_produce timer uses "shards" while sibling metrics use "shard"
findings.body: The `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` timer is tagged `tags={"shards": shard_tag}` while `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` in the same function use `tags={"shard": shard_tag}`. Dashboards and queries that slice these metrics by the shard tag will silently miss the wait_produce series (it lands under a different tag name), fragmenting the flusher observability this PR is meant to add.

findings.title: Per-process restart counters are never reset, so lifetime restarts eventually crash the consumer
findings.body: self.process_restarts[process_index] is only ever incremented in _ensure_processes_alive() and never reset, even after a process runs healthily for a long time. The guard `> MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS` (10) therefore counts restarts over the entire consumer lifetime rather than within a failure window. A long-running consumer that legitimately recovers a flusher process a handful of times per quarter will eventually hit the limit and raise RuntimeError, forcing a full consumer restart and Kafka rebalance. The counter should decay or reset after the process has been healthy for some period.

findings.title: _create_process_for_shard (singular) is dead code
findings.body: The method _create_process_for_shard(shard) is never called anywhere; restarts go through _ensure_processes_alive() -> _create_process_for_shards() directly. Dead code with a misleading name that suggests per-shard restarts exist; it should be removed to avoid confusion.

findings.title: Docstring says "one process per shard" but the shipped default is one process total
findings.body: The class docstring states "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the new --flusher-processes CLI option in sentry/consumers/__init__.py defaults to 1, so the default (and typical) deployment runs a single process handling all shards in round-robin groups. The docstring misrepresents the actual behavior and will mislead operators reasoning about parallelism and failure blast radius (one hung process stalls all shards by default).

findings.title: The added time.sleep(0.1) in test_basic is a no-op due to the test's own monkeypatch
findings.body: test_basic monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a lambda returning None at the top of the test, which patches the time module globally. The later `time.sleep(0.1)` added "to give flusher threads time to process after drift change" therefore sleeps for zero time, so the comment is wrong and the intended wait never happens. The assertion `(msg,) = messages` still depends on a race: the flusher thread must observe the new current_drift and complete producing before step.join() sets the stopped flag and the thread exits its `while not stopped.value` loop. The test can flake or silently stop covering the flush path; it should use an unpatched sleep (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr` scoped to the flusher module, or a real sleep via a saved reference).
